20.0.0.en: Hezekiah fell gravely ill, and the prophet Isaiah visited him and informed him that he would die of this illness, and advised him to give his children and servants instructions about what he wanted.

20.1.0.en: Hezekiah turned his face to the wall to pray alone, his face thus being directed toward the temple, which his illness prevented him from reaching, and he implored the Lord, saying: Ah, Lord, remember how I have walked in uprightness and sincerity, and have done what is good in Your sight. And Hezekiah wept bitterly. He begged God to remove the illness from him and not to permit him to die. This shows Hezekiah's faith in God.

20.2.0.en: After Isaiah announced to Hezekiah that his death was at the door, he left the royal palace and walked in the city of Jerusalem, and minutes later, before he reached the middle of the city, God declared new words to him, that he should return and say them to Hezekiah. God's answer was very swift: He heard with concern the prayer of Hezekiah, which came from the depths of his heart and his contrition before God, which appeared in his tears. So He said to Isaiah: I will heal him of his illness quickly, so that he will recover completely and, after three days, will be able to fulfill his desire, which is to worship before Me and pray in My holy temple. God answers quickly the fervent prayers and spiritual longings, mingled with material requests, of His children who love Him; for Hezekiah does not want healing only, but to enjoy being in the temple of God and praying before Him there.

20.2.1.en: Hezekiah's illness unto death, then his healing after three days, is a type of the death of Christ and His resurrection, by which He gave us the grace of entering His sanctuary, that is, His Church, and partaking of her sacraments, and then entering the Kingdom, just as Hezekiah entered and prayed in the temple of God.

20.2.2.en: Hezekiah wept with tears that God might remove death from him, and Christ offered up prayers and supplications, with strong crying and tears, to Him who was able to save Him (Heb 5:7). Christ thus expresses the difficulty of the cup of suffering that He had to pass through for our redemption.

20.3.0.en: The Lord's answer was swift and specific, for He promised Hezekiah an additional fifteen years of life. This is divine generosity in giving, as long as the one who prays is one of His godly children. He also promises to deliver him from the king of Assyria and to preserve Jerusalem, Hezekiah's capital. Therefore many consider that this event, although it was written in the Bible after the killing of Sennacherib and his army, took place before that, that is, before the siege of Jerusalem, or at least during it. The illness and the healing may also have taken place after the victory over Sennacherib, and God's promise here would be to preserve him and his city from any other attack by Assyria.

20.3.1.en: God affirms that His preserving of Hezekiah and Jerusalem is for the glorifying of the name of God and for the sake of the prayers and blessing of David, the godly servant of God, and this confirms the doctrine of the intercession of the saints. Also God's saying, "I will deliver you and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria," shows that God delivers Jerusalem for the sake of Hezekiah's godliness, and this is a second confirmation of the intercession and blessing of the saints.

20.3.2.en: Here we see how God blesses His children and adds to their lifespan. By human nature, Hezekiah should have died, but God prolonged his days because of his godliness and God's love for him.

20.3.3.en: On the other hand, God does not bless the wicked. Sennacherib, the unjust and hard-hearted, because of his blasphemy against God, saw his army perish by divine destruction at the hand of the angel; then Sennacherib died in a way he could not have expected, killed by his two sons inside the temple of his pagan god, on whom he had relied, which became the cause of his destruction.

20.3.4.en: Ask God in faith, confident of His love for you, and He will give to you generously because He loves you. And seek the intercession of the saints, because they have a great standing with Him, and He rejoices in your friendship with them.

20.4.1.en: Isaiah gave the prescription for healing to those around the sick Hezekiah, which was that they should put a lump of figs on the abscess that he might recover; so they laid it on the boil, and Hezekiah was healed.

20.4.2.en: The lump of figs was not the source of the healing, but a visible material means through which the grace given by God can be felt. In the same way our Church, according to the commandments of the Gospel, practices the sacraments of the Church through visible material things behind which are hidden the divine graces that God grants to the one who receives the sacrament. In the sacraments, materials such as water and oil are used; and of old Elisha used salt and flour in his miracles, and Christ Himself used clay in healing the man born blind, because man needs tangible things to support his faith.

20.5.0.en: Hezekiah asked whether there was a sign the Lord would give him confirming that he would be healed, so that he could rise and go to pray in the house of the Lord, which his heart desired. This means that he recovered within three days.

20.6.0.en: Isaiah answered him: Here is a sign to reassure you that the Lord will do what He promised; so answer me first, shall the shadow go forward ten degrees, or go back ten degrees?

20.7.0.en: Hezekiah said to himself that the shadow goes forward, and this appears on the sundial, so he asked God that the sign be contrary to nature, which is the shadow's going back, that is, that it should not go forward but return backward ten degrees. The degrees are those that Ahaz arranged by means of a pillar with steps on it, each step showing a division of time, so that when the shadow goes forward or goes back it appears on this pillar, which is what is called the sundial of Ahaz (Isa 38:8).

20.8.0.en: Isaiah cried to the Lord, and He brought the shadow back by the degrees by which it had gone forward, the degrees of Ahaz, ten degrees.

20.8.1.en: This miracle has a deep meaning: it means that God is able to change the order of nature, which is what He did by the resurrection of the Savior after the death on the Cross, giving us a sign of eternal life, in the resurrection of us all from death. It also shows that God is ready to change the whole world for the sake of His children whom He loves. The going back of the shadow means the going back of Hezekiah's age to youth, so that he lived with vitality for fifteen years, with energy and strength.

20.8.2.en: The going back of the shadow was not in Jerusalem only, but in the whole world, and when it happened and the Babylonians and Egyptians observed it, they were greatly alarmed, and learned afterwards that this was because of Hezekiah's prayer, so they were certain of his godliness and his standing with God.

20.9.0.en: At that time, that is, in the days of Hezekiah, and that was either before the paying of silver and gold to Assyria or after his victory. Although his treasuries were empty, they were filled with gifts from the surrounding kings, in honor of him after the sun moved for his healing (2 Chr 32:23). The kingdom of Babylon, subject to the Assyrian empire, began to grow strong and tried to show its influence, and in the end it was able to overcome Assyria and to dominate the world. King Merodach of Babylon tried to establish relations with the surrounding states in order to reduce Assyria's dominion. When he heard of Hezekiah's recovery from his illness, accompanied by the going back of the shadow, that is, that the sun which they worshiped had honored Hezekiah, and he also heard that heaven had been with him in his victory over the Assyrian army, he tried to win his favor by sending him letters of praise and showing concern for his health and his kingdom, and even sent him a gift.

20.10.0.en: When the letters of Babylon arrived with the envoys to Hezekiah, and he saw the gift and the king of Babylon's exalting of him, he became proud in his heart, and instead of glorifying God and ascribing the credit to Him, he felt his own strength and thought of allying with Babylon, which was gradually growing strong, and wanted to show his wealth. So he showed his great possessions to the envoys of Babylon, whether gold and silver, or luxuries, or military strength, and in this he stole the glory of God and ascribed it to himself. This is completely different from his attitude when the letters of Assyria came to him, and how he humbled himself before God in humility, so God gave him victory over Sennacherib.

20.10.1.en: The visit of the envoys of Babylon was an opportunity for Hezekiah to proclaim the name of his God and glorify Him before the nations, that perhaps they might believe. He ought to have made clear to them the power of God that appeared in the victory over Sennacherib, and then in his healing, instead of being proud, relying on his wealth and strength. For when man relies on himself, he forgets God, and when he relies on God, he forgets himself.

20.10.2.en: And he did not take refuge in the prophet Isaiah to seek his counsel, but was proud and relied on his strength, and so he sinned. Had he asked Isaiah, he would have kept him from this error and preserved him from its evil consequences.

20.10.3.en: If God has bestowed virtues and blessings on you and you have felt them in your life, do not speak much about that, but thank God and hide your virtues, as you hide your sins. And if you want to proclaim your virtues, would you agree to proclaim your sins first?!

20.11.0.en: Isaiah went to Hezekiah to alert him to his sin, and asked him who had visited him and from where, and he told him that they were envoys of Babylon who had come from afar to visit him. Isaiah asked him, What have they seen in your house? Hezekiah answered, They have seen all my treasuries and all the glory that is in my house. Here Isaiah does what God did with Adam when He called to him in the garden after the Fall, saying to him, Where are you? to call him to repentance. Isaiah tries to alert Hezekiah, that he may feel his sin and his pride and his attempt to ally with Babylon rather than rely on God.

20.12.0.en: Since Hezekiah did not take heed of his sin, Isaiah declared to him God's punishment: because of his pride and his displaying of his wealth and glory before the envoys of Babylon, a time would come when they would carry all his wealth, and what his fathers, the former kings, had stored up, to Babylon; and more than this, Babylon would not only plunder the wealth of Jerusalem, but would take the royal seed, to become slaves to the king of Babylon.

20.13.0.en: Hezekiah felt his sin and humbled himself in repentance (2 Chr 32:24-26), and submitted to the divine judgment and thanked God, because all this chastening would not happen in his days, but after him. This indeed happened in the days of his son Manasseh, who walked in evil.

20.13.1.en: Hezekiah tried to rely on Babylon and ally with it, and this ruin came upon him. So do not try to rely on the world and its strength, lest many troubles befall you. Rely on God alone, for He will keep you and deliver you from all evil.

20.14.0.en: The rest of the acts of Hezekiah and all his achievements and the building works he carried out, such as making the pool and the conduit and bringing water into the city (Jerusalem), are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the kings of Judah. Then Hezekiah died and was buried with his fathers, and his son Manasseh reigned in his place.

20.14.1.en: Remember every day that you will leave this world, and prepare for your eternity by repentance, love for God and doing good to all who are around you.

20.14.2.en: The life of Hezekiah king of Judah is recorded in the Bible in (2 Kgs 18:1-20:21, 2 Chr 29:1-32:33, Isa 36:1-39:8).

20.14.3.en: 1- Hezekiah is a Hebrew name meaning "the Lord has strengthened."

20.14.4.en: 2- He was born in 740 BC in Jerusalem.

20.14.5.en: 3- Ahaz, the father of Hezekiah, began to reign with his father Jotham in 736 BC, when Hezekiah was four years old. Ahaz was wicked, but his kingdom was strong.

20.14.6.en: 4- Ahaz died and his son Hezekiah reigned alone in 716 BC; Hezekiah had reigned for a period with his father Ahaz.

20.14.7.en: 5- Hezekiah removed everything connected with the worship of idols; he destroyed the altars built on the high places and the idols, and also cut down the groves and crushed the bronze serpent (ch. 18:4).

20.14.8.en: 6- He opened the doors of the temple, which had been shut in the days of his father Ahaz (2 Chr 29:3), and began the worship himself and encouraged the people, who followed his example (2 Chr 29:20).

20.14.9.en: 7- He cared for the restoration of the house of the Lord, which had been ruined and neglected in the days of his father Ahaz (2 Chr 29:3).

20.14.10.en: 8- He gathered the priests and the Levites and commanded them to sanctify themselves for the service of the house of the Lord, and charged them to remove the uncleanness from it (2 Chr 29:5), and he organized their divisions (2 Chr 31:2) and commanded them to attend to the feasts and festivals according to the Law (2 Chr 31:3-10).

20.14.11.en: 9- He made military preparations to face the Assyrian army, building forts and fortresses around Jerusalem. He arranged the water supply of the city by digging a conduit from the pool of Gihon to supply the city, surrounded it with a new wall, and attended to the arming of his soldiers (2 Chr 32:3, 4), and encouraged his people against Assyria, because God was with them (2 Chr 32:7, 8).

20.14.12.en: 10- He gave much of his wealth for the daily burnt offerings of the house of the Lord and encouraged the people to give, and they gave abundantly (2 Chr 30:24, 31:5, 6).

20.14.13.en: 11- He took care to keep the Passover in the kingdom of Judah, and even invited the remnant from the kingdom of Israel to share with them (2 Chr 30:2, 15).

20.14.14.en: 12- He took care to have the Psalms of David sung at worship in the house of the Lord and encouraged the people to do so, and they sang with the musical instruments of David (2 Chr 29:27, 30).

20.14.15.en: 13- He took care for the upright conduct of his people, so he collected the proverbs of Solomon from chapter twenty-five until

20.14.16.en: 14- Hezekiah fell ill and prayed to God, and He healed him and extended his life by fifteen years (ch. 20:1, 5, 6), and that was in 701 BC.

20.14.17.en: 15- Merodach, son of Baladan, king of Babylon, congratulated him on his recovery and presented him with a gift (ch. 20:12), and that was in 701 BC.

20.14.18.en: 16- Hezekiah showed his treasuries to the envoys of Babylon, and God punished him through Isaiah by the carrying off of these possessions to Babylon, because of Hezekiah's pride (ch. 20:13, 17, 18).

20.14.19.en: 17- Sennacherib attacked and seized the cities of Judah in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah (ch. 18:13).

20.14.20.en: 18- Hezekiah was afraid and paid gold and silver to Sennacherib and declared his submission to him, so that he would leave Jerusalem (ch. 18:14).

20.14.21.en: 19- Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem, and Hezekiah prayed and spread the Assyrian letters of threat in the house of the Lord (ch. 19:14).

20.14.22.en: 20- Isaiah reassured Hezekiah that God would deliver him from Assyria (ch. 19:20).

20.14.23.en: 21- The angel of the Lord killed a hundred and eighty-five thousand of the Assyrian army, and that was in 701 BC; Sennacherib fled, and his two sons killed him in the temple of his god (ch. 19:35-37).

20.14.24.en: 22- Hezekiah died, after God extended his life by fifteen years, so that he had reigned twenty-nine years, and that was in 686 BC, and his son Manasseh succeeded him (ch. 20:21). Manasseh king over Judah and his son Amon
